gap: No result ChatGPT got states that the mic-sensitivity figures for these six products come in four different, non-comparable forms. Only HyperX (-42 dBV re 1 V/Pa) and Maono (XLR -52 dBV; USB -10.5 dBFS/Pa at max gain) name a reference. EKSA (-42 ±3 dB), FIFINE (-50 ±3 dB) and Antlion ModMic (-36 ±3 dB) give bare dB. So ChatGPT's line that a standalone mic gives 'usually better' voice quality can't be checked against the spec sheets. The one stated figure that does separate two products is the ModMic's 9 dB S/N gap between its two capsules (uni 67 dB vs omni 58 dB).
standout_why: ChatGPT's chat (2026-11-08) got no search results and cited no pages, so there is no rival page to compare against. Its answer is a generic headset-vs-mic table ('Decent' vs 'Usually better', 'Requires setup') with no product, spec, unit or number. Our current page also has no sensitivity or S/N figures, and it doesn't flag that the EKSA's '7.1' and 'noise cancelling' claims depend on which cable you use and which product page you read.
decides: This confirms ChatGPT's split but changes the reason. The spec sheets can't rank headset mics against desk mics, because only HyperX and Maono state a reference. What normalises cleanly: (1) the Maono PD200XS's USB figure is a digital output level at full gain, while its XLR figure (-52 dBV) is 10 dB below the headset capsules' -42 dBV. That 10 dB is the dynamic capsule's lower output, which is why it needs to be 2 to 4 in. from the mouth, and it is not a quality score. (2) If the shopper picks the ModMic, use the cardioid (uni) capsule: Antlion's own figures give it 9 dB better S/N than the omni. (3) The EKSA E900 Pro's 7.1 surround is a PC-plus-USB-driver feature, so on Xbox or Switch over 3.5 mm it is a stereo headset. Its mic is called 'Cardioid' on one EKSA page and 'Omnidirectional' on another, so the 'noise cancelling' claim shouldn't decide anything.

findings.note: From Maono's spec block (read through the store's product data): 'Sensitivity XLR:-52dBV USB:-10.5dBFS/Pa(Max)'. dBV is an analog output level, re 1 V at 1 Pa.

findings.label: Mic sensitivity, USB
findings.note: dBFS is a digital level: 1 Pa (94 dB SPL) reaches -10.5 dB below digital full scale with the gain knob at max. The gain range is stated as 0 to +42 dB, so at minimum gain that works out to about -52.5 dBFS/Pa (-10.5 - 42). That is our arithmetic, assuming the knob's range is linear in dB. This figure can't be compared directly with any dBV figure in this table.

findings.label: How the sensitivity figures normalise
findings.value: 2 of 6 products state a reference (HyperX dBV re 1 V/Pa; Maono dBV for XLR and dBFS/Pa at max gain for USB). 3 give bare '±3 dB'. 1 (Maono DGM20) wasn't read.
findings.note: Our footnote, built from the rows above. Taking the stated dBV figures only: headset electrets at -42 dBV put out 10 dB more voltage at 1 Pa than the PD200XS dynamic at -52 dBV. That means less preamp gain is needed, but it says nothing about voice quality or keyboard rejection, both of which depend on mic distance and pattern. A dBFS figure is set after the mic's own gain stage, so the Maono USB figure can't be put on the same scale as the others.
